ME 8990 - Time Series Forecasting

Chapter 3Time Series Graphics

Every forecasting model we build later in this course (ETS, ARIMA, regression, neural forecasters) encodes assumptions about trend, seasonality, and serial dependence. Graphics are how we find out which of those assumptions are defensible before fitting anything. A model fitted to data you have never looked at is a model you cannot defend.

13 sections 10 figures 27 code cells ~11 min read

3.1Learning objectives#

By the end of this lecture you should be able to:

  1. Represent a time series in pandas with an appropriate time index (Timestamp vs. Period), and identify the index, key, and measured variables of a tidy time series table.
  2. Produce and interpret the five core exploratory graphics: time plot, seasonal plot, seasonal subseries plot, scatterplot, and lag plot.
  3. Distinguish trend, seasonality, and cyclic behaviour, and explain why the distinction matters for model selection.
  4. Compute and read the autocorrelation function (ACF), and recognise the ACF signatures of trend, seasonality, and white noise.
  5. Recognise data that are not worth modelling (white noise) and data with multiple seasonal periods.

3.3Time series data in pandas#

A time series is a sequence of numerical observations together with information about when each observation was recorded. In pandas we hold both pieces in a DataFrame: one or more columns carry the when, and one or more columns carry the what.

Start from an ordinary table of annual observations.

In [3]
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Year": list(range(2015, 2020)),
    "Observation": [123, 39, 78, 52, 110],
})
df
Year Observation
0 2015 123
1 2016 39
2 2017 78
3 2018 52
4 2019 110

3.3.1Index and columns#

Every DataFrame has an index (row labels) and columns (column labels). By default the index is a RangeIndex, which carries no information. For time series work we usually want time to be the index.

3.3.2Timestamps and Periods#

pandas offers two ways to represent time, and the distinction matters for seasonal data.

pd.Timestamp pd.Period
Meaning an instant in time an interval of time
"2020-01" becomes 2020-01-01 00:00:00 the whole month of January 2020
Index type DatetimeIndex PeriodIndex
Best for irregular, high-frequency, or trading-day data regularly spaced calendar data (monthly, quarterly)

Monthly sales are really an interval quantity (a total accumulated over the month), so a Period is the honest representation. In practice, most Python forecasting tooling expects a DatetimeIndex with timestamps pinned to the start of each interval. Just remember that a monthly observation dated 2020-01-01 means "January 2020", not "1 January 2020".

In [7]
print(repr(pd.Timestamp("2020-01")))   # an instant: midnight, 1 Jan 2020
print(repr(pd.Period("2020-01")))      # an interval: the month of January 2020

Timestamp('2020-01-01 00:00:00')
Period('2020-01', 'M')
In [8]
print(repr(pd.Timestamp("2020")))
print(repr(pd.Timestamp("2020-01-01 12:34")))
print(repr(pd.Period("2020-01-01")))            # daily frequency inferred
print(repr(pd.Period("2020-01-01", freq="M")))  # forced to monthly

Timestamp('2020-01-01 00:00:00')
Timestamp('2020-01-01 12:34:00')
Period('2020-01-01', 'D')
Period('2020-01', 'M')

3.4Time plots#

For time series data, the obvious graph to start with is a time plot: observations against time, with consecutive observations joined by straight lines. It is the first thing you draw, always.

Example: weekly economy-class passenger numbers between Melbourne and Sydney.

In [13]
melsyd_economy = (
    pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "ansett.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
    .loc[lambda x: (x["Airports"] == "MEL-SYD") & (x["Class"] == "Economy")]
    .rename(columns={"Airports": "unique_id"})
    .assign(y=lambda x: x["y"] / 1000)
)
melsyd_economy.head()
ds unique_id Class y
3881 1987-06-29 MEL-SYD Economy 20.167
3882 1987-07-06 MEL-SYD Economy 20.161
3883 1987-07-13 MEL-SYD Economy 19.993
3884 1987-07-20 MEL-SYD Economy 20.986
3885 1987-07-27 MEL-SYD Economy 20.497
In [14]
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 3))
plt.plot(melsyd_economy["ds"], melsyd_economy["y"], color="blue")
plt.xlabel("Week in 1987 - 1993")
plt.ylabel("Passengers (x 1k)")
plt.title("Ansett Airlines economy class: Melbourne–Sydney")
plt.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)
plt.show()

What the plot tells us. A single graph already raises several questions that no summary statistic would have surfaced:

  • There was a period in 1989 when no passengers were carried -- an industrial dispute.
  • There was a period of reduced load in 1992 -- a trial in which economy seats were replaced by business class.
  • A large increase in load in the second half of 1991.
  • Large dips at the start of each year -- a holiday effect.
  • A level shift in 1993 and a change in volatility toward the end of the series.

Any forecasting model for this series has to deal with these events. In practice, you would model the periods separately, or introduce intervention variables, rather than pretend the whole record came from one stable process. Plotting the data is what makes that decision possible.

Notice the pattern: a graphical feature → a mechanism in the real world → a modelling decision. That chain is the whole point of exploratory graphics.

3.5Time series patterns#

In describing these time series, we often use terms, e.g., trend and seasonality, which require further clarification.

Trend. A long-term increase or decrease in the data. It need not be linear, and it may change direction (a "changing direction" trend).

Seasonality. A pattern that repeats over a fixed and known period, e.g., time of year, day of the week, hour of the day. Seasonality is always of a fixed and known frequency.

Cycle. Rises and falls that are not of a fixed frequency, usually related to economic or business conditions. Cycles typically last at least two years and their duration varies.

Many series contain more than one pattern at a time. The four panels below show different combinations.

In [15]
hsales = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "hsales.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
ustreas = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "ustreas.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
aus_production = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "aus_production.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))

axes[0, 0].plot(hsales["ds"], hsales["y"], color="blue")
axes[0, 0].set(title="US new one-family houses sold",
               ylabel="Total sales ('000)", xlabel="Month")

axes[0, 1].plot(np.arange(1, len(ustreas) + 1), ustreas["y"], color="red")
axes[0, 1].set(title="US treasury bill contracts",
               ylabel="Price", xlabel="Day")

elec = aus_production.loc[aus_production["ds"] >= "1980"]
axes[1, 0].plot(elec["ds"], elec["Electricity"], color="green")
axes[1, 0].set(title="Australian quarterly electricity production since 1980",
               ylabel="GWh", xlabel="Quarter")

beer = aus_production.loc[aus_production["ds"] >= "1975"]
axes[1, 1].plot(beer["ds"], beer["Beer"], color="orange")
axes[1, 1].set(title="Australian beer production since 1975",
               ylabel="Million Packages", xlabel="Quarter")

plt.show()

Read the four panels carefully:

  1. US housing sales: strong seasonality within each year, plus cyclic behaviour with a period of roughly 6–10 years. There is no apparent long-run trend over this window.
  2. US treasury bills: a downward trend over 100 consecutive trading days. If the record were longer, that decline would be revealed as part of a cycle; the apparent trend is an artefact of the observation window.
  3. Australian electricity production: a strong increasing trend with strong seasonality; no evidence of cyclic behaviour.
  4. Beer production: a strong seasonality and a cyclical pattern over a multi-year horizon, accompanied by a long-term upward trend in production volume. This exhibits classic multi-component time series structure, and forecasting typically requires methods that capture both seasonal variations and trend dynamics.

3.6Seasonal plots#

A seasonal plot is like a time plot, except that the data are plotted against the individual "seasons" (months, quarters, hours) with a separate line for each year. It makes the shape of the seasonal pattern obvious, and shows immediately in which years the pattern departed from the norm.

In [16]
hsales_seasonal = hsales.assign(
    Year=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.year,
    Month_num=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.month,
)
years = sorted(hsales_seasonal["Year"].unique())
year_palette = dict(zip(years, sns.color_palette("husl", n_colors=len(years))))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
sns.lineplot(data=hsales_seasonal, x="Month_num", y="y",
             hue="Year", palette=year_palette, legend=False, ax=ax)

# Label the end of each year's line
for year, g in hsales_seasonal.groupby("Year"):
    g = g.sort_values("Month_num")
    ax.text(g["Month_num"].iloc[-1] + 0.12, g["y"].iloc[-1], str(year),
            ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8, weight="bold",
            color=year_palette[year])

ax.set(
    title="Seasonal plot: US new one-family houses sold",
    xlabel="Month", ylabel="Total sales ('000)",
    xlim=(0.7, 13.2),
    xticks=range(1, 13),
    xticklabels=["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                 "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"],
)
plt.show()

3.7Seasonal subseries plots#

A seasonal subseries plot collects the data for each season into a separate mini time plot and draws the seasonal mean as a horizontal line. Where a seasonal plot emphasises the shape within a year, a subseries plot emphasises how each individual season changes over the years, which is the underlying seasonal trend.

In [17]
hsales_sub = hsales.assign(
    year=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.year,
    month_idx=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.month,
    month_abbr=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.strftime("%b"),
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 12, figsize=(11, 5), sharey=True)
for ax, ((_, abbr), g) in zip(axes, hsales_sub.groupby(["month_idx", "month_abbr"])):
    ax.plot(g["year"], g["y"], color="red", lw=1)
    ax.axhline(g["y"].mean(), color="blue", lw=1.4)
    ax.set(title=abbr, xlabel="")
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=90, labelsize=7)

fig.supxlabel("Month")
fig.supylabel("Total sales ('000)")
plt.show()

The blue lines are the monthly means. Two things stand out:

  • Every month shows fluctuations across the years rather than a uniform monotonic increase. The cyclical swings are present across all months, reflecting the broader housing market cycles.
  • The mean level varies across months, with a peak in the spring/summer months and lower sales volume during winter months.

If a subseries plot showed one month rising while another fell, the seasonal pattern itself would be changing over time, and a model with fixed seasonal indices would be indefensible.

3.8Scatterplots#

The graphics so far have looked at one series at a time. Scatterplots explore the relationship between series, which is what we need whenever a forecasting model will use predictor variables.

We use half-hourly electricity demand and temperature for Victoria in 2014.

In [18]
vic_elec = pd.read_csv("data/vic_elec.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True)

for ax, uid, label in [(axes[0], "Demand", "Demand (MWh)"),
                       (axes[1], "Temperature", "Temperature (°C)")]:
    g = (vic_elec.loc[vic_elec["unique_id"] == uid]
         .sort_values("ds")
         .tail(2 * 24 * 365))          # last year of half-hourly data
    ax.plot(g["ds"], g["y"], color="blue", lw=0.4)
    ax.set(ylabel=label)

axes[0].set_title("Time-series plots of electricity demand and temperature: Victoria, 2014")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Time [30 min]")
plt.show()
In [19]
elec_2014 = (
    vic_elec.loc[lambda x: x["ds"].dt.year == 2014]
    .pivot(index="ds", columns="unique_id", values="y")
    .reset_index()
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
sns.scatterplot(data=elec_2014, x="Temperature", y="Demand",
                ax=ax, linewidth=0, s=8, alpha=0.4, color="red")
ax.set(
    title="Scatterplot of electricity demand vs. temperature, Victoria 2014",
    xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Electricity demand (MWh)",
)
plt.show()

The relationship is strongly non-linear: demand is lowest around 16–18 °C and rises on both sides; mildly at low temperatures (heating) and very steeply above about 25 °C (air conditioning). The two arms of the U are not symmetric: the cooling arm is far steeper than the heating arm.

A linear regression of demand on temperature would be badly misspecified, and the correlation coefficient on its own would never tell you so.

3.9Correlation#

The correlation coefficient measures the strength of the linear relationship between two variables $x$ and $y$:

$$ r \;=\; \frac{\sum (x_t - \bar{x})(y_t - \bar{y})} {\sqrt{\sum (x_t - \bar{x})^2}\;\sqrt{\sum (y_t - \bar{y})^2}} $$

with $-1 \le r \le 1$. Two warnings that matter enormously in practice:

  1. $r$ measures linear association only. The demand–temperature relationship above is very strong but U-shaped, so a single $r$ badly understates it, and the number you get depends on how much of each arm of the U happens to be in your sample.
  2. $r$ can be identical for wildly different data. Anscombe's quartet is the classic demonstration.
In [20]
def r_of(mask, label):
    s = elec_2014.loc[mask]
    r, _ = pearsonr(s["Temperature"], s["Demand"])
    print(f"{label:<22} r = {r:+.3f}   (n = {len(s):>6,})")

temp = elec_2014["Temperature"]
r_of(temp.notna(), "All data")
r_of(temp < 18, "Below 18 °C")
r_of(temp >= 20, "20 °C and above")
print("\nMean demand by 2-degree temperature bin (MWh):")
print(
    elec_2014
    .assign(bin=(temp // 2) * 2)
    .groupby("bin")["Demand"].mean().round(0)
    .to_string()
)

The overall $r = +0.28$ fairly describes neither regime. Above 20 °C the linear relationship is strong ($r = +0.70$); below 18 °C it is essentially absent ($r = -0.14$). The binned means make the asymmetry explicit: mean demand falls from about 4,800 MWh near freezing to a minimum of about 4,300 MWh at 16–18 °C, then more than doubles to about 9,200 MWh at 42 °C.

3.10Lag plots#

A lag plot is a scatterplot of a series against itself, shifted by $k$ periods: the horizontal axis holds $y_{t-k}$ and the vertical axis holds $y_t$. It is the visual counterpart of autocorrelation.

We use quarterly Australian beer production from 2000 onwards, colouring each point by the quarter of the current observation.

In [21]
beer = (
    pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "aus_production.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
    [["ds", "Beer"]]
    .loc[lambda x: x["ds"] >= "2000"]
    .assign(Season=lambda x: "Q" + x["ds"].dt.quarter.astype("string"))
    .rename(columns={"Beer": "y"})
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
beer.head()
ds y Season
0 2000-01-01 421 Q1
1 2000-04-01 402 Q2
2 2000-07-01 414 Q3
3 2000-10-01 500 Q4
4 2001-01-01 451 Q1
In [22]
lims = 0.95 * beer["y"].min(), 1.05 * beer["y"].max()
seasons = ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"]
colors = dict(zip(seasons, plt.get_cmap("viridis")(np.linspace(0, 1, 4))))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(8, 7), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for i, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    lag = i + 1
    d = beer.assign(lagged=beer["y"].shift(lag))
    sns.scatterplot(data=d, x="lagged", y="y", hue="Season",
                    hue_order=seasons, palette=colors, ax=ax, s=25, legend=False)
    ax.plot(lims, lims, color="0.5", ls="--", lw=1, zorder=-1)
    ax.set(title=f"lag {lag}", xlabel="", ylabel="")

handles = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=colors[s], label=s) for s in seasons]
axes[1, -1].legend(handles=handles, loc="center left", title="Season",
                   bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 0.5), frameon=False, borderaxespad=0)
fig.suptitle("Lag plots: Australian quarterly beer production (2000–2010)")
fig.supxlabel("lag(Beer, k)")
fig.supylabel("Beer (megalitres)")
plt.show()

The lag plots encode the seasonality directly:

  • Lags 4 and 8 show a strong positive relationship: the same quarter in successive years behaves alike ($m = 4$ for quarterly data).
  • Lags 2 and 6 show a strong negative relationship: Q4 peaks are paired with Q2 troughs.
  • The colours make the mechanism explicit; at lag 4 each colour stays on the 45° line, because Q1 is compared with Q1, Q2 with Q2, and so on.

A lag plot that shows tight, structured scatter is telling you that past values carry information about future values. That information is exactly what a forecasting model exploits.

3.11Autocorrelation#

Autocorrelation measures the linear relationship between a series and its own lagged values. It is the numerical summary of a lag plot. The lag-$k$ autocorrelation coefficient is

$$ r_k \;=\; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t=k+1}^{T} (y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t-k} - \bar{y})} {\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{T} (y_t - \bar{y})^2} $$

where $T$ is the length of the series. The collection $\{r_1, r_2, r_3, \dots\}$ is the autocorrelation function (ACF), and the plot of $r_k$ against $k$ is a correlogram.

In [23]
acf_vals = sm.tsa.acf(beer["y"], nlags=9, fft=False, bartlett_confint=False)
acf_df = pd.Series(acf_vals, name="ACF").to_frame().rename_axis("lag")
acf_df[1:]  # lag 0 is always 1 by construction
ACF
lag
1 -0.052981
2 -0.758175
3 -0.026234
4 0.802205
5 -0.077471
6 -0.657451
7 0.001195
8 0.707254
9 -0.088756
In [24]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
plot_acf(beer["y"], lags=16, ax=ax, zero=False,
         bartlett_confint=False, auto_ylims=True, color="k")
ax.set(title="ACF: Australian quarterly beer production",
       xlabel="lag [1Q]", ylabel="ACF")
plt.show()

Compare this correlogram with the lag plots: $r_4$ is the largest positive value and $r_2$ the most negative, exactly as the lag plots showed. The scalloped shape, i.e., peaks every four lags, alternating with troughs, is the ACF signature of quarterly seasonality.

The shaded band is the significance region. Spikes reaching outside it indicate autocorrelation that is unlikely to have arisen by chance.

3.11.1Trend and seasonality in ACF plots#

Two rules of thumb that you should be able to apply on sight:

  • Trend: the ACF decays slowly and stays positive for many lags, because observations nearby in time are similarly far from the mean.
  • Seasonality: the ACF shows peaks at multiples of the seasonal period $m$.

When both are present you see both: a slow decay with a scalloped ripple superimposed.

3.12White noise#

A time series that shows no autocorrelation is called white noise. It is the reference case: it contains no exploitable structure, so the best possible forecast of its next value is its mean.

In [25]
rng = np.random.RandomState(30)
wn = pd.DataFrame({
    "unique_id": "White noise",
    "ds": np.arange(1, 51),
    "y": rng.normal(0, 1, 50),
})

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3))
plt.plot(wn["ds"], wn["y"], color="blue", lw=1)
plt.xlabel("Sample [1]")
plt.ylabel("y")
plt.title("White noise")
plt.grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)
plt.show()
In [26]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
plot_acf(wn["y"], lags=16, ax=ax, zero=False,
         bartlett_confint=False, auto_ylims=True, color="k")
ax.set(title="ACF: white noise", xlabel="lag [1]", ylabel="ACF")

T = len(wn)
bound = 1.96 / np.sqrt(T)
print(f"T = {T},  ±1.96/√T = ±{bound:.3f}")
plt.show()

T = 50,  ±1.96/√T = ±0.277

For white noise we expect each $r_k$ to be close to zero. More precisely, for a series of length $T$, the sample autocorrelations of white noise lie within

$$ \pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{T}} $$

about 95 % of the time. Those are the dashed bounds drawn on every correlogram.

How to read the bounds. If all spikes lie inside the band, the series is consistent with white noise and there is nothing to model. But be careful: each individual spike has about a 5 % chance of falling outside the band even when the series is pure noise, so a single marginal excursion is not evidence of structure. The simulation below shows how often that happens with 20 lags. What you should react to is a pattern of excursions, which is a slow decay, or spikes at multiples of $m$.

In [27]
# How often does pure noise breach the bounds? (a quick simulation)
rng2 = np.random.RandomState(7)
n_reps, T, n_lags = 2000, 50, 20
bound = 1.96 / np.sqrt(T)
breaches = [
    np.sum(np.abs(sm.tsa.acf(rng2.normal(size=T), nlags=n_lags, fft=False)[1:]) > bound)
    for _ in range(n_reps)
]
print(f"Mean number of spikes outside the band, out of {n_lags} lags: {np.mean(breaches):.2f}")
print(f"Share of simulated white-noise series with ≥1 breach: {np.mean(np.array(breaches) >= 1):.1%}")

Mean number of spikes outside the band, out of 20 lags: 0.52
Share of simulated white-noise series with ≥1 breach: 36.8%

3.13Summary#

Graphic Built from Reveals
Time plot $y_t$ vs. $t$ trend, seasonality, cycles, outliers, level shifts, changing variance
Seasonal plot $y_t$ vs. season, one line per year shape of the seasonal pattern; unusual years
Seasonal subseries plot one mini time plot per season, plus seasonal means how each season evolves over the years
Scatterplot $y_t$ vs. $x_t$ relationships between series; non-linearity; outliers
Lag plot $y_t$ vs. $y_{t-k}$ serial dependence; seasonality
ACF / correlogram $r_k$ vs. $k$ numerical summary of serial dependence; trend and seasonality signatures

Things to carry into the rest of the course:

  1. Plot before you model. Every modelling decision later in this course, e.g., transformation, differencing, seasonal period, choice of predictors, is justified by something you can see in one of these six graphics.
  2. Seasonality is fixed-period; cycles are not. They call for different model components.
  3. Increasing seasonal amplitude with level: consider a log or Box–Cox transformation, or a multiplicative decomposition.
  4. Slowly decaying ACF: trend, likely non-stationary, likely needs differencing.
  5. Spikes at multiples of $m$ in the ACF: seasonality of period $m$.
  6. All spikes inside $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$: white noise; there is nothing left to forecast. This is what you want to see in model residuals.
